name: Bura
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Blench, Roger. 2009. Bura phonology and some suggestions concerning the orthography. Draft circulated for comment, printout 10 July 2009. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. 9 pp. (i + 7 + references). Open PDF from the author's site, the Internet Archive capture 2015-04-20 ofhttps://www.rogerblench.info/Language/Afroasiatic/Chadic/Central/Bura/Bura%20phonology.pdf
catalog_quote: Like most Nigerian languages, Bura is a tone language. Its tone system is yet to be fully worked out. Davies (1954-56) pointed to a three-way tone contrast as follows; ká swear / ka and, with / kà let, may … Almost certainly, however, Bura has two tones and downstep. Downstep is a tone which sounds like high tone but which has the effect of lowering the tones of the rest of the sentence. Such systems are very common in Chadic languages. Downstep often sounds like a mid-tone and this may well be its historical origin. Downstep is typically marked with ! in phonology, but this is not very helpful in practical orthography. Bura has phonetic rising tone caused by sequences of two vowels with different tones. For example; However, it seems to have rare phonemic rising tone. For example; The tones are shown as follows; High ʹ / Low ˋ / Falling ˆ / Rising ˇ Where words differ only in tone, they are listed in the order high, low.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: No source opened says anything about word stress or accent. The only prosodic statement is that Bura is a tone language with (probably) two lexical tones H and L plus downstep, rare phonemic rising tone, and phonetic rises across vowel sequences (Blench 2009). Schuh's 1981-82 wordlist marks lexical tone on every headword (H, L, falling on some, e.g. tlâata), corroborating lexical tone contrast; Blench's 2010 dictionary draft marks tone only sporadically and leaves its 'Phonology' heading empty. The mission grammar notes (Bura Grammar for a Beginner) mention tone only once (possessive pronoun constructions).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: Davies (1954-56, the 'Biu Book') posited a three-way tone contrast which Blench reinterprets as two tones plus downstep; tone marking is described as unsettled ('yet to be fully worked out').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone (minimal sets ká/ka/kà; dictionary headwords). Blench 2009 is a circulated draft, not a peer-reviewed publication, based on a 2009 Jos lexicography workshop and mission materials from the Garkida area; Maddieson 1983 and Schuh's list are based on a single Garkida speaker (Elisha Shalanguwa). None of the opened sources treats Pabir separately.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened materials describe Bura proper (Garkida / Biu-area mission variety; Schuh's and Maddieson's data from one Garkida speaker, Elisha Shalanguwa; Blench's from the 2009 Jos workshop with the Bura Literacy Committee). Glottolog bura1292 'Bura-Pabir' also covers Pabir (Babur); no opened source treats Pabir separately or gives it a distinct prosody. No dialect-level glottocode applies.

tone_statements.citation: Gutzmann, Daniel, Katharina Hartmann & Lisa Matthewson. 2020. Verum focus is verum, not focus: Cross-linguistic evidence. Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 5(1): 51, 1-48. doi:10.5334/gjgl.347
tone_statements.quote: In this section we address verum expression in two Central Chadic languages (Bura, cf. Hartmann, Jacob & Zimmermann 2008; Hartmann & Zimmermann 2012), and South Marghi (cf. Hartmann 2013). Both languages have SVO as their base order. They are tone languages and differentiate a high and a low tone. In the following, only high tones are represented, by accents on the vowels.
tone_statements.locator: p. 18 (Art. 51, page 18 of 48), section 4.2; fn. 12 on the same page: tones are not marked on some field-note examples from Bura and South Marghi
tone_statements.check: quotation from a journal article located by the 2026-09-24 journal search, not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: The paper is about how verum (emphasis on the truth of a proposition) is marked and argues it is a lexical operator rather than focus; for Bura it shows verum marked by particles and word order, not by tone or accent. sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. with Elisha Shalanguwa. 2010 [data 1981-82]. Bura-English-Hausa Dictionary. Unpublished ms., Los Angeles (Unicode export 17 Aug 2010), c. 1500-1600 tone-marked headwords.
sources.note: Introduction covers orthography and the two classes of word-final vowels (stable vs. deleted/reduced to schwa phrase-medially); headwords carry tone marks (H, L, falling), but there is no statement on stress or on the tone system.
